title: Servers & Backend
summary: Learn how the backend of every app works: HTTP, building servers and REST APIs in Node.js, databases, logging, scaling, Linux and security.

lessons.title: What is a server?
lessons.summary: Meet the computer program that waits for requests and answers them.

slides.title: A program that waits
slides.text:
**A server** is a program that:
- starts and keeps running
- **listens** for requests
- sends back **responses**

The word also means the computer it runs on.
slides.narration: Let us start with the big idea. A server is simply a program that starts, keeps running, and waits for someone to ask it for something. When a request arrives, it does some work and sends back an answer. People also use the word server for the machine that runs such programs.

slides.title: Clients and servers
slides.text:
- **Client**: asks (browser, phone app, another program)
- **Server**: answers

One server can talk to **thousands** of clients at once.
slides.narration: The program that asks is called the client. Your browser is a client, so is a phone app, and so is a script that calls an API. One server usually serves many clients at the same time, which is why servers must be fast and careful.

slides.title: Addresses and ports
slides.text:
A client finds a server by:
- **host**: a name like `example.com` or an IP like `93.184.215.14`
- **port**: a number like `80`, `443` or `3000`

DNS turns names into IP addresses.
slides.narration: To reach a server, a client needs two things: the address of the machine and a port number. The address can be a name, which DNS turns into an IP address. The port tells the machine which program should get the message, because one computer can run many servers at once.

slides.title: Frontend vs backend
slides.text:
- **Frontend**: what runs in the browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript)
- **Backend**: what runs on the server (logic, data, security)

The backend is where secrets and databases live.
slides.narration: You will often hear the words frontend and backend. The frontend is the part users see, running on their device. The backend runs on the server, where it keeps data, checks permissions and holds secrets that must never be sent to the browser.

slides.title: Kinds of servers
slides.text:
- **Web / API servers**: pages and data over HTTP
- **Database servers**: store and query data
- **File, mail, game, DNS servers**

This course focuses on **web and API servers**.
slides.narration: There are many kinds of servers. Database servers store data, mail servers move email, game servers keep players in sync. In this course we focus on web and API servers, the backbone of almost every modern app.

lessons.notes:
## What is a server?

A **server** is a program that runs continuously and **listens** for requests from other programs, called **clients**. When a request arrives, the server does some work (reads data, saves something, runs a calculation) and sends a **response** back.

The word "server" is also used for the computer that runs these programs, often a machine in a data center or a virtual machine in the cloud.

## The client/server model

| Client | Server |
|---|---|
| Starts the conversation | Waits for requests |
| Browser, mobile app, script | Node.js, Python, Java, Go program |
| Many of them | Usually few, shared by all |

## How clients find servers

- **Host**: a domain name (`api.example.com`) or an IP address.
- **DNS** translates names into IP addresses.
- **Port**: a number from 0 to 65535 that picks which program on the machine gets the message. HTTP uses **80**, HTTPS uses **443**, and during development we often use **3000** or **8080**.

A full address looks like `https://api.example.com:443/users`.

## Frontend and backend

- **Frontend** code runs on the user's device. Anyone can read it, so it must never contain secrets.
- **Backend** code runs on the server. It talks to databases, checks who the user is, and enforces the rules.

## Key ideas

- A server is always on and reacts to requests.
- Clients and servers talk using agreed rules called **protocols**; on the web that protocol is **HTTP**.
- One server handles many clients, so speed, reliability and security matter a lot.

quiz.q: What does a server mainly do?
options: Waits for requests and sends responses
quiz.explain: A server listens for requests from clients and answers each one.

quiz.q: Which of these is a client?
quiz.explain: The browser starts the conversation by sending requests, so it is a client.

quiz.q: What is the port number for?
options: It picks which program on a machine receives the message
quiz.explain: One machine can run many servers; the port tells it which program should get the data.

lessons.task: Open three apps or websites you use daily. For each one, write down: who is the client, what the server probably stores, and one request the client sends (for example "load my messages").

lessons.title: HTTP requests and methods
lessons.summary: Learn what an HTTP request looks like and what GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE mean.

slides.title: HTTP is plain text rules
slides.text:
HTTP is the language of the web.

A request has:
- a **request line**
- **headers**
- an optional **body**
slides.code:
GET /users?id=3 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
slides.narration: HTTP is the set of rules clients and servers use to talk on the web. Each request starts with one request line, then some headers, then an optional body with data.

slides.title: The request line
slides.text:
`METHOD  PATH?QUERY  VERSION`

- **method**: what to do
- **path**: which resource
- **query**: extra options after `?`
slides.narration: The first line says three things. The method says what you want to do. The path says which resource you mean. Anything after the question mark is the query string, with extra options like filters or page numbers. Finally comes the protocol version.

slides.title: The main methods
slides.text:
- **GET**: read
- **POST**: create / send data
- **PUT**: replace
- **PATCH**: change part
- **DELETE**: remove
slides.narration: There are five methods you will use all the time. GET reads data. POST creates something or sends data to be processed. PUT replaces a resource completely, PATCH changes part of it, and DELETE removes it.

slides.title: Safe and idempotent
slides.text:
- **Safe**: does not change data (GET, HEAD)
- **Idempotent**: repeating it has the same effect (GET, PUT, DELETE)
- **POST** is neither: sending twice may create two orders
slides.narration: Two words help you choose methods well. A safe method does not change anything on the server. An idempotent method can be repeated with the same result, which matters when a network retries a request. POST is neither, so clicking buy twice might create two orders.

slides.title: Headers and body
slides.text:
- Headers: `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Accept`, `Cookie`
- Body: the data, often **JSON**

The response has a **status line**, headers and a body too.
slides.narration: Headers carry extra information, such as the type of data in the body or who the user is. The body carries the data itself, usually JSON for APIs. The server answers with the same shape: a status line, headers and a body.

slides.title: HTTP versions in 2026
slides.text:
- **HTTP/1.1**: text, still everywhere
- **HTTP/2**: binary, many requests on one connection
- **HTTP/3**: runs over **QUIC** (UDP)

The methods and status codes are the same in all of them.
slides.narration: You may hear about HTTP 2 and HTTP 3. They change how bytes travel, making things faster, but the ideas you learn here, methods, paths, headers and status codes, stay exactly the same.

lessons.notes:
## Anatomy of a request

```http
POST /api/orders?notify=true HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer abc123

{"item": "book", "qty": 2}
```

1. **Request line**: method `POST`, target `/api/orders?notify=true`, version `HTTP/1.1`.
2. **Headers**: `Name: value` pairs.
3. A blank line.
4. **Body**: the data.

The target splits into a **path** (`/api/orders`) and a **query string** (`notify=true`). Query strings hold `key=value` pairs joined by `&`.

## Methods

| Method | Meaning | Safe | Idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | read a resource | yes | yes |
| HEAD | like GET, headers only | yes | yes |
| POST | create / process data | no | no |
| PUT | replace a resource | no | yes |
| PATCH | change part of a resource | no | not guaranteed |
| DELETE | remove a resource | no | yes |
| OPTIONS | ask what is allowed (used by CORS) | yes | yes |

## Responses

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/orders/77

{"id": 77, "item": "book", "qty": 2}
```

## Versions

HTTP/1.1 is text based. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (over QUIC) send the same messages in a faster binary form. Your server code rarely needs to care: frameworks and proxies handle it.

quiz.q: In `GET /books?page=2 HTTP/1.1`, what is the path?
quiz.explain: The path is the part of the target before the question mark.

quiz.q: Which method should you use to remove a resource?
quiz.explain: DELETE asks the server to remove the resource.

quiz.q: Why is POST not idempotent?
options: Repeating it may create a second resource
quiz.explain: Sending the same POST twice can create two orders, so repeating it changes the result.

lessons.title: Status codes
lessons.summary: Read the three-digit number that tells the client how its request went.

slides.title: Every response has a code
slides.text:
The status line starts every response:

`HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found`

The **first digit** tells you the family.
slides.narration: Every response begins with a status code, a three digit number with a short phrase. The first digit is the most important, because it tells you the family of the answer.

slides.title: The five families
slides.text:
- **1xx** Informational
- **2xx** Success
- **3xx** Redirection
- **4xx** Client error
- **5xx** Server error
slides.narration: There are five families. One hundreds are informational and rare. Two hundreds mean success. Three hundreds mean go somewhere else. Four hundreds mean the client did something wrong, and five hundreds mean the server failed.

slides.title: Codes you will use daily
slides.text:
- **200** OK, **201** Created, **204** No Content
- **301/308** moved permanently, **302/307** temporary, **304** Not Modified
- **400** Bad Request, **401** Unauthorized, **403** Forbidden, **404** Not Found
- **500** Internal Server Error, **503** Unavailable
slides.narration: Here are the codes you will see every day. Two hundred is plain success, two oh one means something was created, and two oh four means success with no body. Four oh one means we do not know who you are, while four oh three means we know you, but you are not allowed.

slides.title: More useful 4xx
slides.text:
- **405** Method Not Allowed
- **409** Conflict (e.g. duplicate email)
- **422** Unprocessable Content (validation failed)
- **429** Too Many Requests (rate limit)
slides.narration: A few more client errors make APIs much clearer. Four oh five means the path exists but not with that method. Four oh nine signals a conflict, four twenty two says the data failed validation, and four twenty nine tells a client it is sending too many requests.

slides.title: Pick the honest code
slides.text:
Bad: `200 OK` with `{"error": "not found"}`

Good: `404 Not Found` with `{"error": "user 7 not found"}`

Tools, caches and clients **rely** on the code.
slides.narration: A common beginner mistake is to always reply two hundred and put the error inside the body. Do not do that. Browsers, caches, monitoring tools and client code all read the status code first, so it must tell the truth.

lessons.notes:
## Status code families

| Range | Family | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 100-199 | Informational | keep going, switching protocols |
| 200-299 | Success | it worked |
| 300-399 | Redirection | look somewhere else / use your cache |
| 400-499 | Client error | the request is wrong |
| 500-599 | Server error | the server failed |

## The ones to remember

- **200 OK**: normal success.
- **201 Created**: a POST created something; add a `Location` header.
- **204 No Content**: success with an empty body (common for DELETE).
- **301 / 308**: moved permanently. **302 / 307**: moved temporarily. 307 and 308 keep the method.
- **304 Not Modified**: the client's cached copy is still fresh.
- **400 Bad Request**: malformed input, e.g. broken JSON.
- **401 Unauthorized**: not logged in (the name is historical; it means *unauthenticated*).
- **403 Forbidden**: logged in but not allowed.
- **404 Not Found**: no such resource.
- **405 Method Not Allowed**, **409 Conflict**, **422 Unprocessable Content**, **429 Too Many Requests**.
- **500 Internal Server Error**: a bug or crash.
- **502 Bad Gateway / 504 Gateway Timeout**: a proxy could not get a good answer from the server behind it.
- **503 Service Unavailable**: overloaded or under maintenance.

## Good habits

- Always send the most specific honest code.
- Send a JSON body with a human-friendly `error` message for 4xx and 5xx.
- Never leak stack traces in a 500 response; log them on the server instead.

quiz.q: A user is logged in but tries to delete someone else's post. Which code fits best?
quiz.explain: 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you lack permission.

quiz.q: Which family means the server itself failed?
quiz.explain: 5xx codes signal a server-side error.

quiz.q: What does 201 mean?
quiz.explain: 201 Created is the usual answer to a successful POST that made a new resource.

lessons.title: Your first Node.js server
lessons.summary: Write a tiny HTTP server with Node.js and run it from the terminal.

slides.title: Node.js runs JavaScript on servers
slides.text:
**Node.js** runs JavaScript outside the browser.

It ships with a built-in `http` module, so you need **no extra packages** to start.
slides.narration: Node js lets JavaScript run outside the browser, which makes it a popular choice for servers. It comes with a built in module called http, so we can build a working server without installing anything.

slides.title: The whole server
slides.text: Save this as `server.js`:
slides.narration: Here is a complete server in about ten lines. It creates a server, gives it a function to run for every request, and tells it to listen on port three thousand.

slides.title: Line by line
slides.text:
- `createServer(fn)`: `fn` runs **for every request**
- `req`: what the client sent (`method`, `url`, `headers`)
- `res`: what you send back
- `writeHead` sets status and headers, `end` sends the body
slides.narration: The function you pass to create server is called once per request. The req object describes the request, and the res object is how you answer. Write head sets the status code and headers, and end sends the body and finishes the response.

slides.title: Run it in the terminal
slides.text:
```
node server.js
```
Then open **http://localhost:3000** in a browser.

The program **keeps running**. Stop it with **Ctrl + C**.
slides.narration: Because a server never finishes on its own, you must run it in a terminal, not with a quick run button. Type node server dot js, then open localhost port three thousand in your browser. To stop the server, press control and C in the terminal.

slides.title: Test with curl
slides.text:
```
curl -i http://localhost:3000/hello
```
`-i` shows the status line and headers too.

Tip: `node --watch server.js` restarts on every save.
slides.narration: You can also test with curl, a command line client. The dash i flag prints the status line and headers, so you see the full response. And during development, node dash dash watch restarts the server every time you save the file.

slides.title: Frameworks
slides.text:
Real projects often use a framework on top of `http`:
- **Express** (most common)
- **Fastify** (fast, schema based)
- **Hono** (small, runs on many platforms)
slides.narration: For real projects most people use a framework that sits on top of the http module. Express is the most common, Fastify focuses on speed, and Hono is tiny and runs almost anywhere. They all do the same basic job you just saw, with nicer tools for routing and errors.

quiz.q: How often does the function passed to `http.createServer` run?
quiz.explain: The handler is called for each incoming request.

quiz.q: What happens if you forget `res.end()`?
options: The client waits and never gets a finished response
quiz.explain: end() finishes the response; without it the client hangs until a timeout.

quiz.q: How do you stop a server running in the terminal?
quiz.explain: Ctrl + C sends an interrupt signal that stops the Node process.

lessons.task:

2. Change the message and the status code, restart, and check with `curl -i http://localhost:3000`.

lessons.title: Routing
lessons.summary: Send each method and path to the right piece of code, including paths with parameters.

slides.title: One server, many pages
slides.text:
A **route** = method + path → handler

- `GET /` → home
- `GET /users` → list users
- `GET /users/:id` → one user
- `POST /users` → create user
slides.narration: A real server answers many different requests. A route connects a method and a path to the code that should handle it. Routing is the job of choosing the right route for each request.

slides.title: Routing by hand
slides.text: With plain Node you check `req.method` and `req.url` yourself.
slides.narration: With plain Node you can route by hand with if statements. It works, but it becomes messy fast, especially once paths contain values like user ids.

slides.title: Path parameters
slides.text:
Pattern `/users/:id` matches `/users/42`.

- Split both by `/`
- Same number of parts?
- `:name` parts capture a value
- Other parts must be equal
slides.narration: Many routes contain a changing value, like a user id. We write the route as a pattern with a colon, like slash users slash colon id. To match, split both the pattern and the path at the slashes, check they have the same number of parts, capture the parts that start with a colon, and require the rest to be equal.

slides.title: 404 vs 405
slides.text:
- No route has this **path** → **404 Not Found**
- Path exists, but not for this **method** → **405 Method Not Allowed**
slides.narration: When nothing matches, be precise. If no route has that path at all, answer four oh four. If the path exists but only for other methods, answer four oh five, and ideally list the allowed methods in an Allow header.

slides.title: Routing in Express
slides.text: Frameworks do all of this for you.
slides.narration: Frameworks like Express do this matching for you. You declare routes with the method name, and the captured values appear in req dot params.

lessons.notes:
## What routing is

A **router** looks at each request's **method** and **path** and picks a **handler** function. Order matters: most routers try routes from top to bottom and use the first match.

## Matching a pattern

Route patterns use `:name` for parameters.

| Pattern | Path | Match? | Params |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/users/:id` | `/users/42` | yes | id=42 |
| `/users/:id` | `/users` | no (different length) | |
| `/users/:id/posts/:pid` | `/users/7/posts/3` | yes | id=7, pid=3 |
| `/users/me` | `/users/42` | no (`me` ≠ `42`) | |

Algorithm:

1. Split pattern and path by `/`.
2. If the number of parts differs, no match.
3. For each part: if the pattern part starts with `:`, store the value; otherwise the parts must be equal.

## Query strings are separate

`/users?page=2` still matches `/users`. Use `new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost')` and read `url.searchParams.get('page')`.

## 404 or 405?

- **404**: no route matches the path.
- **405**: a route matches the path, but not with this method. Send an `Allow: GET, POST` header.

## With a framework

```js
app.get('/users', listUsers);
app.post('/users', createUser);
app.get('/users/:id', getUser);
app.delete('/users/:id', deleteUser);
```

Put specific routes such as `/users/me` **before** general ones such as `/users/:id`, or the general one will catch them first.

quiz.q: Does `/users/:id` match `/users/10/posts`?
options: No, the number of parts differs
quiz.explain: The pattern has 2 parts and the path has 3, so they do not match.

quiz.q: The path `/orders` exists only for GET. A client sends DELETE /orders. Best response?
quiz.explain: The path exists but not for that method: 405 Method Not Allowed.

quiz.q: Why put `/users/me` before `/users/:id`?
options: Otherwise `/users/:id` would catch `me` as an id
quiz.explain: Routers use the first match, so the general pattern would swallow the specific one.

lessons.title: REST APIs and JSON
lessons.summary: Design clean APIs around resources and exchange data as JSON.

slides.title: What is an API?
slides.text:
An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a server that answers **programs**, not people.

It usually sends **JSON** instead of HTML pages.
slides.narration: An API is a server built for programs instead of people. A mobile app, a website, or another server sends requests and gets back data, usually as JSON, rather than full web pages.

slides.title: JSON in one slide
slides.text:
- objects `{ }`, arrays `[ ]`
- strings in **double quotes**
- numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`
- no comments, no trailing commas
slides.narration: JSON is a simple text format for data. It has objects in curly braces, arrays in square brackets, strings in double quotes, numbers, true, false and null. It does not allow comments or trailing commas, which trips up many beginners.

slides.title: REST: resources and verbs
slides.text:
**Nouns** in the URL, **verbs** in the method:
- `GET /books` list
- `POST /books` create
- `GET /books/7` read one
- `PATCH /books/7` update
- `DELETE /books/7` delete
slides.narration: REST is a popular style for designing APIs. The idea is to put nouns, the resources, in the URL, and use the HTTP method as the verb. So you never write a path like slash delete book; you send DELETE to slash books slash seven.

slides.title: Parse and validate
slides.text:
In JavaScript:
- `JSON.parse(text)` → value (throws on bad JSON)
- `JSON.stringify(value)` → text

**Never trust input.** Check types and ranges, reply **400** or **422** on bad data.
slides.narration: In JavaScript, JSON dot parse turns text into a value and throws an error if the text is broken, and JSON dot stringify does the opposite. Always validate what clients send: check that fields exist and have the right types, and answer with a four hundred family code when they do not.

slides.title: Good API habits
slides.text:
- plural nouns, lowercase: `/orders`
- **versioning**: `/v1/orders`
- **pagination**: `?page=2&limit=20`
- consistent errors: `{"error": "..."}`
- document it with **OpenAPI**
slides.narration: A few habits make APIs pleasant to use. Use plural lowercase nouns, add a version to the path so you can change things later, paginate long lists, and return errors in the same shape every time. Describe the whole API with an OpenAPI document so others can read and test it.

lessons.notes:
## APIs and REST

An **API** lets programs talk to your server. **REST** is a design style where:

- each **resource** has a URL (`/books`, `/books/7`),
- the **HTTP method** says what to do,
- the server is **stateless**: each request carries everything needed (for example a token),
- responses use honest **status codes**.

| Action | Request | Success code |
|---|---|---|
| List | `GET /books` | 200 |
| Create | `POST /books` | 201 + `Location` |
| Read | `GET /books/7` | 200 |
| Replace | `PUT /books/7` | 200 or 204 |
| Update part | `PATCH /books/7` | 200 |
| Delete | `DELETE /books/7` | 204 |

## JSON in JavaScript

```js
const text = '{"title":"Dune","year":1965}';
const book = JSON.parse(text);   // object
book.year += 1;
console.log(JSON.stringify(book)); // {"title":"Dune","year":1966}
```

`JSON.parse` **throws** on invalid input, so wrap it in `try/catch` and answer **400 Bad Request**.

## Validation

Check every field: does it exist, is it the right type, is it in range? Answer **400** for malformed JSON and **422** (or 400) for well-formed JSON with invalid values. Libraries like **Zod** or JSON Schema validators help in larger projects.

## Other API styles

- **GraphQL**: one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs.
- **gRPC**: fast binary calls between services.
- **WebSockets / Server-Sent Events**: live updates pushed from the server.

REST with JSON remains the most common choice for public web APIs.

quiz.q: Which is the most RESTful way to delete book 7?
quiz.explain: REST uses the method as the verb and the URL as the resource.

quiz.q: Which is valid JSON?
quiz.explain: JSON requires double-quoted keys and strings and no trailing commas.

quiz.q: What does JSON.parse do with broken text?
quiz.explain: JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError, so handle it with try/catch.

exercise.title: Validate a POST body
exercise.prompt:
You are writing the handler for `POST /users`. Standard input is the raw request body (one line).

- If it is not valid JSON, or not a JSON **object**, print `400` then `{"error":"invalid JSON"}`.
- Else if `name` is missing, not a string, or empty after trimming, print `422` then `{"error":"name is required"}`.
- Else if `age` is not an integer from 0 to 150, print `422` then `{"error":"age must be an integer from 0 to 150"}`.
- Otherwise print `201` then the new user as JSON with keys in this order: `{"id":1,"name":<trimmed name>,"age":<age>}`.

Use `JSON.stringify` to print the JSON line.

tests.output:
422
{"error":"age must be an integer from 0 to 150"}

lessons.title: Middleware
lessons.summary: Run shared steps such as logging, parsing and auth before your route handlers.

slides.title: Shared steps for every request
slides.text:
Many requests need the **same steps**:
- log the request
- parse the JSON body
- check the user is logged in
- add security headers

**Middleware** = small functions that run in a chain.
slides.narration: Lots of routes need the same steps: logging, reading the body, checking who the user is. Instead of copying that code into every handler, we write small functions called middleware and run them in a chain before the route.

slides.title: The chain
slides.text:
Each middleware can:
- read or change `req` / `res`
- call `next()` to continue
- or **end** the response early (e.g. 401)
slides.narration: Each middleware gets the request, the response and a function called next. It can look at or change the request, then call next to pass control along. Or it can stop the chain by sending a response itself, for example a four oh one when no token is present.

slides.title: Using it in Express
slides.text:
`app.use()` applies to all routes.
Pass middleware to a single route too.
slides.narration: In Express, app dot use adds middleware for every request, in the order you write it. You can also attach middleware to a single route, which is handy for checks like requiring a login only on private pages.

slides.title: Order matters
slides.text:
`logger → json → auth → route → error handler`

The **error handler** comes last and has **4 arguments**: `(err, req, res, next)`.
slides.narration: Order matters a lot. The body parser must run before a route that reads the body, and auth must run before private routes. At the very end you add an error handling middleware, which in Express has four arguments, so any thrown error becomes a clean five hundred response.

slides.title: Common middleware
slides.text:
- body parsing (`express.json()`)
- CORS
- security headers (**helmet**)
- rate limiting
- compression
- request IDs for logs
slides.narration: You rarely write all middleware yourself. There are well tested packages for body parsing, CORS, security headers, rate limiting and compression. Your job is to pick them, order them correctly, and write the few that are specific to your app.

lessons.notes:
## The idea

**Middleware** is a function that sits between the incoming request and your route handler. In Express the signature is:

```js
function name(req, res, next) { /* ... */ next(); }
```

A middleware can:

1. **Inspect or change** `req` and `res` (e.g. attach `req.user`).
2. Call **`next()`** to hand over to the next middleware.
3. **End** the request early with a response (e.g. `401`, `429`).

## A typical stack

```js
app.use(requestId);       // tag each request with an ID
app.use(logger);          // log method, path, status, duration
app.use(helmet());        // security headers
app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://app.example.com' }));
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));
app.use('/api', apiRouter);
app.use(notFound);        // 404 for anything left
app.use(errorHandler);    // (err, req, res, next)
```

## Error handling

```js
function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) {
  console.error(err);                       // full details in the log
  res.status(500).json({ error: 'Something went wrong' });
}
```

In Express 5, errors thrown inside `async` handlers are passed to the error handler automatically.

## Tips

- Keep each middleware small and focused on one job.
- Always either call `next()` **or** send a response, never both and never neither.
- Limit body size to protect the server from huge uploads.
- Other frameworks (Fastify hooks, Hono middleware, Django/Flask in Python) use the same idea under different names.

quiz.q: What must a middleware do if it does not send a response?
quiz.explain: Calling next() passes control to the next function in the chain.

quiz.q: Where should the error-handling middleware go?
quiz.explain: It must come after the routes so it can catch their errors.

quiz.q: What is special about an Express error handler?
quiz.explain: Express recognizes error handlers by their (err, req, res, next) signature.

lessons.task:
On paper (or in a text file), design the middleware stack for a small notes API with these needs: every request is logged, JSON bodies are parsed, `/api/notes` routes need a logged-in user, anything else gives 404, and crashes return a friendly 500.

Write the `app.use(...)` lines in the right order and explain in one sentence why each one is placed where it is.

lessons.title: Databases from the backend
lessons.summary: Store data safely with SQL, parameterized queries, connection pools and migrations.

slides.title: Why a database?
slides.text:
Variables vanish when the server restarts.

A **database** stores data **permanently** and lets many servers share it.
- **SQL**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite
- **NoSQL**: MongoDB, Redis, DynamoDB
slides.narration: Anything you keep in a variable disappears when the server restarts, and other servers cannot see it. A database stores data permanently and safely. Relational SQL databases such as PostgreSQL are the most common default, while NoSQL databases fit special cases.

slides.title: Query from Node
slides.text: Use a driver like `pg` for PostgreSQL:
slides.narration: Your backend talks to the database through a driver library. Here we ask PostgreSQL for one user. Notice the dollar one placeholder: the value is sent separately from the SQL text.

slides.title: Never build SQL with strings
slides.text:
**Bad**: `"... WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`

Input `x' OR '1'='1` changes your query: **SQL injection**.

**Good**: placeholders (`$1`, `?`) always.
slides.narration: Never glue user input into SQL text. A crafted input can change the meaning of your query and leak or delete data. This attack is called SQL injection. Placeholders send values separately, so the database never treats them as code.

slides.title: Connection pools
slides.text:
Opening a DB connection is slow.

A **pool** keeps a few connections open and **reuses** them.

Set a sensible maximum (e.g. 10 per server).
slides.narration: Opening a database connection takes time, so servers keep a pool of open connections and reuse them for each request. Keep the pool size modest, because the database can only handle so many connections at once.

slides.title: Migrations and ORMs
slides.text:
- **Migrations**: versioned files that change the schema step by step
- **ORM / query builder**: Prisma, Drizzle, Knex, Sequelize
- **Transactions**: all-or-nothing groups of changes
slides.narration: As your app grows, you change the database structure with migrations, small numbered files kept in version control. Many teams use an ORM or query builder such as Prisma or Drizzle. And when several changes must succeed or fail together, wrap them in a transaction.

lessons.notes:
## Where data lives

The server process is temporary; the **database** is the long-term memory. Typical choices:

- **PostgreSQL**: powerful open-source relational database; a great default.
- **MySQL / MariaDB**: widely used relational databases.
- **SQLite**: a file-based database, perfect for small apps and tests.
- **Redis**: in-memory key-value store, used for caches, sessions and queues.
- **MongoDB**: document database storing JSON-like records.

## Safe queries

```js
// NEVER do this
pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'");

// Always do this
pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]);
```

Placeholders (`$1` in PostgreSQL, `?` in MySQL/SQLite) stop **SQL injection**.

## Connection settings

Keep the connection string in an **environment variable** (`DATABASE_URL`), never in your code or Git. Use a **pool** so connections are reused.

## Transactions

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
```

If anything fails, `ROLLBACK` undoes the whole group.

## Migrations and ORMs

- A **migration** is a script like `003_add_email_to_users.sql`. Tools run them in order on every environment.
- **ORMs / query builders** (Prisma, Drizzle, Knex, Sequelize, TypeORM) map tables to objects and generate safe SQL.

## Performance basics

- Add **indexes** on columns you search by.
- Select only the columns you need.
- Avoid the **N+1 problem**: one query per item in a loop. Use a join or `WHERE id = ANY($1)` instead.

quiz.q: What prevents SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Placeholders send values separately so they are never run as SQL.

quiz.q: Why use a connection pool?
options: To reuse open connections instead of opening a new one per request
quiz.explain: Opening connections is slow; a pool reuses them.

quiz.q: Where should the database password live?
options: In an environment variable or secret manager
In the URL of every request
quiz.explain: Secrets belong in environment variables or a secret manager, never in source code.

lessons.task:
Design the tables for a small library API: `books` (id, title, author, year) and `loans` (id, book_id, member_name, due_date).

1. Write the `CREATE TABLE` statements.
2. Write a **parameterized** query that lists loans due before a given date.

lessons.title: Logging and monitoring
lessons.summary: See what your server is doing with structured logs, metrics, traces and alerts.

slides.title: You cannot watch a server
slides.text:
A server runs at 3 a.m. while you sleep.

**Logs** tell you what happened.
**Metrics** tell you how it is doing.
**Traces** show a request's path.
slides.narration: A server runs day and night and nobody is watching the screen. So we make it describe itself. Logs record events, metrics measure things like requests per second, and traces follow a single request across services. Together they are called observability.

slides.title: Access logs
slides.text:
One line per request:

`2026-10-12T09:00:01Z GET /api/users 200 12ms`

Time, method, path, status, duration.
slides.narration: The most basic log is the access log: one line per request with the time, method, path, status code and how long it took. Just from these lines you can spot errors and slow endpoints.

slides.title: Structured logs
slides.text: Log **JSON**, not free text, so tools can search it.
slides.narration: Modern servers log structured JSON instead of free text. Each field has a name, so log tools can filter, for example, all requests with status five hundred on the orders route. In Node, Pino is a popular fast logger.

slides.title: Log levels
slides.text:
`debug` → `info` → `warn` → `error`

- production usually logs **info** and up
- **never** log passwords, tokens or full card numbers
slides.narration: Use log levels to separate noise from signal. Debug is for development, info for normal events, warn for odd but handled situations, and error for real failures. And never write secrets like passwords or tokens into logs.

slides.title: Metrics and alerts
slides.text:
Watch the **golden signals**:
- **latency** (p50, p95, p99)
- **traffic** (requests/s)
- **errors** (% of 5xx)
- **saturation** (CPU, memory)

Alert when they cross a limit.
slides.narration: Metrics are numbers over time. Google's site reliability engineers call four of them the golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Tools like Prometheus and Grafana collect and graph them, and alerts wake someone up when, say, the error rate jumps.

slides.title: Tracing with OpenTelemetry
slides.text:
**OpenTelemetry** is the open standard for logs, metrics and traces.

A **trace** shows each step of one request: API → DB → cache → other service.
slides.narration: When one request touches many services, a trace shows each step and how long it took. OpenTelemetry is the vendor neutral standard for producing traces, metrics and logs, and almost every monitoring tool accepts its data.

lessons.notes:
## The three pillars of observability

| Pillar | Answers | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Logs** | What happened? | Pino, Winston, Loki, Elasticsearch |
| **Metrics** | How is it doing over time? | Prometheus, Grafana, CloudWatch |
| **Traces** | Where did this request spend time? | OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Tempo |

## Good logging

```js
const pino = require('pino');
const log = pino();
log.info({ method: 'GET', path: '/api/users', status: 200, ms: 12 }, 'request done');
```

- Log **structured JSON** with consistent field names.
- Add a **request ID** to every line so you can follow one request.
- Use levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.
- Write logs to **stdout**; the platform (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes) collects them.
- **Never** log secrets or sensitive personal data.

## Metrics

Track the **golden signals**:

- **Latency**: how long requests take. Look at percentiles (p95, p99), not just the average, because averages hide slow outliers.
- **Traffic**: requests per second.
- **Errors**: share of responses that are 5xx.
- **Saturation**: CPU, memory, connection pool usage.

## Alerts and health checks

- Expose `GET /health` that returns 200 when the server can serve traffic.
- Alert on symptoms users feel (high error rate, slow responses), not on every warning.
- Write a short runbook for each alert: what it means and what to do.

quiz.q: Why log JSON instead of free text?
options: Tools can search and filter by field
quiz.explain: Structured fields make logs easy to query.

quiz.q: Which should never appear in logs?
quiz.explain: Logs are widely readable and kept a long time, so secrets must never be written there.

quiz.q: Why look at p99 latency, not just the average?
quiz.explain: A small share of very slow requests can hurt many users and is invisible in the average.

exercise.title: Summarize an access log
exercise.prompt:
Each non-empty input line is an access log entry: `TIMESTAMP METHOD PATH STATUS DURATIONms`, for example
`2026-10-12T09:00:01Z GET /api/users 200 12ms`.

Print:

```
requests: <count>
2xx: <n>
3xx: <n>
4xx: <n>
5xx: <n>
avg_ms: <average duration, rounded with Math.round>
slowest: <PATH> (<DURATION>ms)
```

Always print all four status lines. If several requests tie for slowest, use the first one. There is at least one line.

tests.input:
t GET /a 200 50ms
t GET /b 200 50ms
t GET /c 503 20ms

lessons.title: Linux server basics
lessons.summary: Log in with SSH, manage your app as a service and put a reverse proxy in front.

slides.title: Servers run Linux
slides.text:
Most servers run **Linux** (Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky, Amazon Linux).

No desktop: you work in a **terminal** over **SSH**.
slides.narration: The vast majority of servers on the internet run Linux, usually without any graphical desktop. You manage them from a terminal, connecting securely over SSH from your own computer.

slides.title: Connect with SSH
slides.text: Use **keys**, not passwords.
slides.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519          # once, on your laptop
ssh-copy-id deploy@203.0.113.10
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10        # log in
slides.narration: SSH gives you a secure terminal on a remote machine. Create a key pair once, put the public key on the server, and log in with it. Then you can turn off password logins entirely, which blocks most automated attacks.

slides.title: Commands you need
slides.text:
- `ls`, `cd`, `pwd`, `cat`, `less`, `nano`
- `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`
- `ps`, `top` / `htop`, `df -h`, `free -h`
- `ss -tlnp` (who listens on which port)
- `journalctl -u myapp -f` (follow logs)
slides.narration: A handful of commands go a long way. Move around and read files, install updates with apt, check processes, disk and memory, see which programs listen on which ports, and follow your app's logs with journal control.

slides.title: Keep the app running: systemd
slides.text: A **service** starts on boot and restarts after crashes.
slides.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My Node API
After=network.target

[Service]
User=deploy
WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/srv/myapp/.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
slides.narration: If you start node in your SSH session, it dies when you log out. Instead, describe your app as a systemd service. Systemd starts it at boot, restarts it when it crashes and collects its logs.

slides.title: Reverse proxy
slides.text:
Put **Nginx** or **Caddy** in front:
- listens on **80/443**
- handles **HTTPS** certificates
- forwards to your app on `localhost:3000`
- serves static files, compresses, limits
slides.narration: Your app listens on port three thousand, but users connect to ports eighty and four four three. A reverse proxy like Nginx or Caddy sits in front, handles HTTPS certificates, and forwards requests to your app. Caddy even gets free certificates from Let's Encrypt automatically.

slides.title: Basic hardening
slides.text:
- non-root user for the app
- firewall: allow only 22, 80, 443 (`ufw`)
- SSH keys only, no root login
- automatic security updates
slides.narration: Before going live, harden the machine. Run the app as a normal user, not root. Turn on a firewall that only allows SSH and web traffic. Disable password and root logins over SSH, and enable automatic security updates.

lessons.notes:
## Working on a Linux server

You connect with **SSH** and type commands. Learn these first:

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Where am I / list files | `pwd`, `ls -la` |
| Read a file | `cat file`, `less file` |
| Edit a file | `nano file` (or `vim`) |
| Install / update (Debian, Ubuntu) | `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade` |
| Processes | `ps aux`, `top`, `htop` |
| Disk / memory | `df -h`, `free -h` |
| Open ports | `ss -tlnp` |
| Service control | `sudo systemctl status/start/stop/restart myapp` |
| Logs | `journalctl -u myapp -f` |

## SSH keys

```
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id deploy@your-server
```

Then in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` set `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin no`, and restart SSH (keep a second session open while testing).

## Running your app as a service

Create a **systemd** unit (see the slide), then:

```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
```

`Restart=always` brings it back after a crash. Logs go to the journal. Many teams use **Docker** containers instead, but the ideas are the same.

## Reverse proxy with Caddy

```
api.example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:3000
}
```

Caddy automatically gets and renews HTTPS certificates. Nginx is equally popular and uses `proxy_pass http://localhost:3000;` with Certbot for certificates.

## Firewall

```
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
```

Your app's port 3000 stays closed to the internet; only the proxy reaches it.

quiz.q: Why use systemd for your Node app?
options: It starts the app at boot and restarts it after crashes
quiz.explain: A systemd service keeps the app running independently of your SSH session.

quiz.q: What does a reverse proxy like Caddy or Nginx do?
options: Receives traffic on 80/443 and forwards it to your app
quiz.explain: It sits in front, handles HTTPS and forwards requests to the app.

quiz.q: Which firewall setup is best for a typical web server?
quiz.explain: Open only what is needed: SSH for admin, 80 and 443 for web traffic.

lessons.task: If you have Linux, WSL or a Mac terminal, try these locally: `pwd`, `ls -la`, `df -h`, `ps aux | head`. Then write (in a text file) the systemd unit you would use for a Node app living in `/srv/notes-api` that runs `node index.js` as user `notes`, and the two commands to enable and start it.

lessons.title: Scaling and performance
lessons.summary: Handle more users with caching, statelessness, load balancers and queues.

slides.title: When one server is not enough
slides.text:
- **Vertical scaling**: a bigger machine (more CPU, RAM)
- **Horizontal scaling**: **more machines** behind a load balancer

Vertical is simple but has a ceiling.
slides.narration: Sooner or later one server is not enough. You can scale vertically by buying a bigger machine, which is simple but limited. Or you can scale horizontally by running many copies of your app behind a load balancer, which is how large sites grow.

slides.title: Load balancers
slides.text:
A **load balancer** spreads requests across servers:
- round robin / least connections
- **health checks** remove broken servers
- terminates HTTPS
slides.narration: A load balancer receives all traffic and spreads it across your servers, for example in turn, or to whichever is least busy. It runs health checks and stops sending traffic to a server that fails them, so one crash does not take down the site.

slides.title: Stateless servers
slides.text:
Any server must be able to handle any request.

So do **not** keep sessions or uploads in server memory or local disk.

Put them in a **database**, **Redis** or **object storage**.
slides.narration: Horizontal scaling only works if your servers are stateless. If a user's session lives in the memory of server A, a request that lands on server B will look logged out. So keep shared state in a database, in Redis, or in object storage.

slides.title: Caching
slides.text:
Do the slow work **once**, reuse the result:
- HTTP caching (`Cache-Control`, ETag)
- **CDN** for static files
- **Redis** cache for hot data

Hard part: knowing when to **invalidate**.
slides.narration: Caching is the cheapest speed boost. Browsers and CDNs can cache responses using headers, and your server can keep hot data in Redis instead of hitting the database each time. The hard part is invalidation: making sure stale data is removed when things change.

slides.title: Queues for slow work
slides.text:
Do not make users wait for:
- sending emails
- resizing images
- generating reports

Put a **job** on a **queue**; a **worker** does it later.
slides.narration: Some work is slow, like sending email or processing video. Do not make the user wait. The web server puts a job on a queue and replies right away, and separate worker processes handle the jobs in the background. If many jobs arrive, you just add more workers.

slides.title: Measure first
slides.text:
1. Measure (metrics, profiling)
2. Find the bottleneck (often the **database**)
3. Fix the biggest one
4. Measure again

Avoid guessing.
slides.narration: Most important of all, measure before you optimize. The bottleneck is very often the database, a missing index, or too many queries. Fix the biggest problem, measure again, and repeat. Guessing wastes time.

lessons.notes:
## Two ways to scale

| | Vertical | Horizontal |
|---|---|---|
| How | bigger machine | more machines |
| Effort | easy | needs stateless design |
| Limit | the largest machine | very high |
| Failure | one box = single point of failure | survives losing one server |

In Node.js, one process uses one main thread. On a multi-core machine run several processes (Node's `cluster` module, PM2, or several containers).

## Load balancing

A load balancer (Nginx, HAProxy, Caddy, or a cloud load balancer) distributes traffic and runs **health checks** like `GET /health`. Unhealthy servers stop receiving traffic.

## Stateless design

- Sessions → Redis or the database (or signed tokens).
- Uploaded files → object storage such as Amazon S3.
- Scheduled jobs → one scheduler, not one per server.

## Caching layers

1. **Browser**: `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`, `ETag` with `304 Not Modified`.
2. **CDN**: copies of static files and cacheable pages near users.
3. **Application cache**: Redis or Valkey for computed results.
4. **Database**: indexes and its own buffer cache.

## Queues and workers

Use a queue (BullMQ with Redis, RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Kafka) for work that can happen later. The API replies `202 Accepted`, the worker finishes the job.

## Database scaling

- Indexes and better queries first.
- **Read replicas** for heavy reading.
- Connection poolers (PgBouncer).
- **Sharding** (splitting data across databases) only when truly needed.

## Rule of thumb

Measure, find the bottleneck, fix it, measure again. Load-test with tools like k6 or autocannon before big launches.

quiz.q: Why must horizontally scaled servers be stateless?
options: Because any server may receive any request
quiz.explain: If state lives on one server, requests routed elsewhere will not see it.

quiz.q: Which task belongs in a background queue?
quiz.explain: Email sending is slow and can happen after the response.

quiz.q: What does a load balancer health check do?
options: Stops sending traffic to servers that fail it
quiz.explain: Health checks let the balancer route around broken servers.

lessons.task: A photo-sharing API is slow at peak time. Users upload photos (resized into 3 sizes), view feeds and get email notifications. Write a short plan: what you would measure first, what you would cache, what you would move to a queue, and how you would make the API servers stateless.

lessons.title: Server security essentials
lessons.summary: Protect your backend with HTTPS, validation, rate limits, safe secrets and updates.

slides.title: Assume the internet is hostile
slides.text:
Bots scan every public server **within minutes**.

Security is layers:
- transport (HTTPS)
- input
- access
- secrets
- updates
slides.narration: As soon as a server is public, automated bots start probing it, often within minutes. No single trick makes you safe, so we build layers: encrypt traffic, distrust input, check access, protect secrets and keep everything updated.

slides.title: HTTPS everywhere
slides.text:
- TLS encrypts traffic and proves the server's identity
- free certificates: **Let's Encrypt**
- redirect HTTP → HTTPS
- add **HSTS** header
slides.narration: Always serve your site over HTTPS. TLS encrypts the traffic and proves to the browser that it is really your server. Certificates are free from Let's Encrypt, and the HSTS header tells browsers to never use plain HTTP for your site again.

slides.title: Never trust input
slides.text:
- validate type, length, format
- parameterized SQL
- escape output in HTML
- limit body and upload size
- check uploaded file types
slides.narration: Every piece of input can be an attack: query strings, headers, JSON bodies and uploaded files. Validate it, use parameterized queries, escape anything you put into HTML, and set limits on size so a giant request cannot knock your server over.

slides.title: Access control on the server
slides.text:
- check **authentication** on every protected route
- check **authorization**: is *this* user allowed to touch *this* record?
- hiding a button in the UI is **not** security
slides.narration: Broken access control is the number one risk on the OWASP Top Ten list. Every protected route must check who the user is and whether they may access that specific record. Hiding a button in the frontend is not protection, because anyone can send the request directly.

slides.title: Rate limits and CORS
slides.text:
- **rate limit** logins and APIs → `429`
- **CORS**: list exactly which sites may call your API from a browser
- security headers via **helmet**
slides.narration: Rate limiting slows down password guessing and abuse, answering four twenty nine when a client sends too much. CORS tells browsers which other websites may call your API, so list specific origins instead of allowing everyone. The helmet package adds sensible security headers in one line.

slides.title: Secrets and updates
slides.text:
- secrets in **env vars** or a **secret manager**, never in Git
- `npm audit`, Dependabot / Renovate
- least privilege for DB users
- backups you have **tested**
slides.narration: Keep API keys and passwords out of your code and out of Git, using environment variables or a secret manager. Update dependencies regularly with tools like npm audit and Dependabot. Give each service only the permissions it needs, and test that your backups can actually be restored.

lessons.notes:
## Layers of defense

1. **Transport**: HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or 1.3, HTTP redirected to HTTPS, `Strict-Transport-Security` header.
2. **Input**: validate everything, limit sizes, use parameterized queries, escape output.
3. **Access**: authenticate users, then authorize every action on every record.
4. **Abuse**: rate limiting, bot protection, request timeouts.
5. **Secrets**: environment variables or a secret manager, rotated regularly.
6. **Supply chain**: keep Node and packages updated; review new dependencies; use a lockfile.
7. **Infrastructure**: firewall, SSH keys only, non-root processes, automatic OS updates.
8. **Recovery**: logs, alerts, tested backups, an incident plan.

## The OWASP Top 10

OWASP publishes the most common web risks. Recent editions are led by **broken access control**, followed by issues like security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures and injection. Read the current list at owasp.org.

## Express example

```js
const helmet = require('helmet');
const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit');
const cors = require('cors');

app.use(helmet());
app.use(cors({ origin: ['https://app.example.com'] }));
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));
app.use('/login', rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, limit: 10 }));
```

## Errors

Return generic messages to clients (`{"error": "Something went wrong"}`) and log full details on the server. Stack traces in responses help attackers.

## Checklist before launch

- [ ] HTTPS only, HSTS on
- [ ] all input validated, SQL parameterized
- [ ] authorization checked per record
- [ ] rate limits on login and expensive endpoints
- [ ] no secrets in the repo; `.env` in `.gitignore`
- [ ] dependencies audited
- [ ] firewall and SSH hardened
- [ ] backups restored once as a test
